items.title: Why I love Rome in winter: ‘We reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines’
items.summary:
There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans

There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole, as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days).

Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. I’d begin with coffee at Gatsby Cafe by Piazza Vittorio before walking along Via Merulana – a tree-lined street similar to a Parisian boulevard – and then through the Colle Oppio park, past the Colosseum and towards Circo Massimo.

items.title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
items.summary:
The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs

One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story.

Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein.

items.title: Why I love Madrid in winter: ‘Locals get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats’
items.summary:
The streets and squares of the Spanish capital come alive with Madrileños shopping, drinking and dining outdoors, warmed by lap blankets and patio heaters

Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle.

Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Many local people get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats, and one of my seasonal highlights is spotting couples or whole families engaged in furious arguments while wearing reindeer antlers or giant turkeys on their heads.

items.title: ‘The spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna’
items.summary:
There’s more to the Austrian capital’s cuisine than schnitzel – its dishes come from all over the world

The Viennese love to eat. That isn’t solely a sign of joie de vivre. Sometimes it’s just hunger. The city has a long history of decline. Entire empires have crumbled here, or simply dissolved. Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, poets quietly starved to death or choked on their own self-importance. Vienna’s cuisine has outlasted them all: a little bit too heavy, a bit too greasy, and always covered in breadcrumbs or sprinkles.

Consider the schnitzel, for example. The Wiener Schnitzel is a legend, supposedly a dish of world-class stature: golden-yellow and wavy, spilling over the plate, with a delicate wedge of lemon daintily nestled beside it (in some of the more upmarket establishments, it even comes wrapped in a little linen pouch). There are few dishes that are so passionately raved about while being so fervently disparaged. The schnitzel has to be pounded until paper-thin, the breadcrumb coating must be light and airy, the accompanying potato salad prepared with a marinade of beef stock, vinegar, oil and finely chopped onions – without (without!) mayonnaise. Anything else is an affront. In Vienna you can get heated debates with strangers about all sorts of ideological nonsense. But the quality of a schnitzel is not up for discussion. items.t: ‘The spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna’

items.title: Vienna on a plate: a food lover’s guide to the Austrian capital
items.summary:
Some of the city’s best chefs, Ola Szwarc, Nadim Amin, Konstantin Filippou and Felix Mandl, share their favourite cafes, bars and restaurants

There are two sides to coffee in Vienna. The grand, old-school coffee houses are incredible places to sit, have breakfast, drink a beer and forget about time. They have much the same function as a pub in Britain. For that experience, we’d go to Café Prückel or Café Hawelka. For a quintessential Viennese coffee, we’d suggest a wiener melange – somewhat similar to a cappuccino, but traditionally a little milder, made with coffee, steamed milk and milk foam. Alternatively, an einspänner is another peculiar, old-fashioned option: a strong black coffee served in a glass with a layer of cold whipped cream on top. items.title: Why I love Stockholm in winter: ‘A return to slowing down, cosying up and revering every glimmer of light’
items.summary:
Swedes adore the festive season, embracing the shorter days with fairy lights, yuletide feasts and fun in the snow

I’ll let you in on a secret: I often tell people that summer is the best time to visit Stockholm. Clouds drift across impossibly blue skies, we skip around midsummer maypoles singing folk songs and cruise the waterways, bobbing and weaving through the archipelago’s 30,000-plus islands.

That’s mostly because I want to keep December in Stockholm to myself. Soft white snow dusts buildings of ochre and burnt sienna like icing on a cake. Festive candles light up pavements leading to cosy cafes, where the earthy, buttery smell of seasonal saffron buns (lussekatter) replaces cinnamon buns for fika, our revered tradition of coffee and cake.

items.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
items.summary:
Ice-skating, illuminated medieval buildings and seasonal treats feature in your picks of atmospheric winter cities

• Tell us about a winter weekend break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher

In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh. The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap.
